headline: Rhode Island charges seven people in Medicaid cases totaling about $1.27 million
dek: The allegations span false claims for services, questionable psychiatric billing and non-emergency medical rides; prosecutors say the cases involved more than $1 million in Medicaid payments.
body: Rhode Island authorities have charged seven people in a group of separate Medicaid-fraud cases that the state says involved more than $1 million in public health payments. The allegations range from claims for services that investigators say were never delivered to transportation bills tied to vehicles or providers who could not have completed the rides.

The cases were announced Oct. 14 by Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha. The figures listed in the attorney general’s release add up to about $1.27 million in alleged improper payments or claims, although the cases are at different stages and the defendants have not been found guilty. Under Rhode Island law, an indictment, information or complaint is an allegation, and each defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty. Source: Rhode Island Attorney General’s Office, https://riag.ri.gov/press-releases/seven-charged-crimes-related-medicaid-fraud-more-1-million.

One of the largest individual allegations involves Erin Burton, 61, of North Providence. The attorney general says Burton submitted about $225,000 in claims for services never rendered to 39 beneficiaries. The listed claims included services supposedly provided to people who were deceased, in a coma or incarcerated when the visits were said to have occurred. Burton faces three Medicaid-fraud counts plus charges of obtaining money under false pretenses and identity fraud.

Another case names Chijioke Nnanna Egbujo, 53, of Farmington, Connecticut. Prosecutors allege that Egbujo, a contracted psychiatrist at Eleanor Slater Hospital, submitted false time records and billing documents for roughly $220,000 in payments. The state says some of the billed services were recorded while Egbujo was absent from the assigned worksite and working at Rhode Island Hospital. A pretrial conference is scheduled for Oct. 22, according to the attorney general.

Two cases involve non-emergency medical transportation, a service Medicaid pays for when eligible patients need rides to care. Moshood Lawal, 48, and Amudat Lawal, 39, are accused of submitting falsified insurance and registration records for their company, Moshlaw Transportation. The state says the company provided 16,000 rides while operating without required insurance and with invalid vehicle registrations, generating about $270,000 in Medicaid reimbursements. Both defendants face Medicaid-fraud and conspiracy charges.

Jessica Dos Santos, 26, of East Providence, is accused of filing about $99,000 in false claims for 15 beneficiaries, including eight members of her own family. She faces Medicaid-fraud, false-pretenses and identity-fraud charges. The attorney general says Dos Santos was arraigned Sept. 9 and has a pretrial conference set for Dec. 9.

The final case names Mustapha Opere Toyin, 44, and Ganait Idris, 46, co-owners of Assured Transportation. Investigators allege that the pair billed Medicaid for rides that could not have occurred as represented, including claims made while one owner was outside the United States and another was hospitalized. The state associated about $453,000 in payments with those claims. Both were charged Oct. 9 and are due for a pre-arraignment conference Nov. 10.

The Rhode Island Attorney General’s Medicaid Fraud Control Unit opened the investigations after referrals from the state Executive Office of Health and Human Services’ Office of Program Integrity. Rhode Island State Police assisted in the Assured Transportation investigation. The unit receives 75% of its funding from the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, a detail that connects the state cases to the broader federal oversight system for Medicaid-provider fraud.

The Newport Buzz independently described the announcement as a series of cases involving alleged billing for dead patients, nonexistent medical appointments and rides that investigators say did not happen as reported: https://thenewportbuzz.com/rhode-island-medicaid-fraud-seven-charged-2026/62886. The U.S. Department of Justice’s 2026 health-care-fraud case summaries also list the Burton and Dos Santos matters: https://www.justice.gov/criminal/criminal-fraud/health-care-fraud-unit/2026-national-hcf-case-summaries. The next steps are court appearances and pretrial proceedings, where prosecutors will have to prove the allegations case by case rather than treating the group announcement as a single prosecution.
